newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO, Russia move closer to new deal.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Russia move closer to new deal.

text.p: NATO and Russia signalled sharply increased cooperation on European security issues on Thursday despite Moscow's bitter opposition to alliance plans to go ahead next year with eastwards expansion.

NATO sources said U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry offered to open the alliance's doors to Moscow in a move which would stop just short of full membership and radically alter the European security architecture of the last 50 years.

"Perry said the allies should be prepared to open up NATO to Russia in virtually every other domain," said one NATO official after a two-day informal meeting of alliance defence ministers in Bergen, Norway.
Other alliance countries saw cooperation in a number of areas, ranging from the struggle against illegal drugs and international crime to the destruction of chemical weapons.

Perry, who earlier stressed the enlargement process would begin next year whatever Moscow said, offered to place Russian liaison officers at every level of the alliance's command structure with permanent offices in each other's headquarters.

NATO hopes a new deal with Russia, enshrined in either a treaty or charter, will result in Moscow dropping its objections to full alliance membership for Russia's old allies from the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who met the ministers for a separate "16+1" session after the main session, repeated Moscow's view that there was "no strategic necessity" to enlarge the alliance.
"Our country does not want the NATO expansion at present... we in our country are concerned," he told a news conference.
Critically, Rodionov also said the dispute over enlargement should not stand in the way of cooperation in other areas, such as Bosnia.
"That (Bosnia) is another matter, one thing is not in contradiction with another," he said in reply to a question.

Rodionov also notably steered clear of the fiery rhetoric that accompanied a virulent anti-enlargement campaign by Moscow last year and said his country was ready to work with NATO on the planning of a possible new peace force for Bosnia.
"We are ready to cooperate," he told reporters.
Perry reportedly told his Russian counterpart that Moscow should be involved in all planning activities for any follow-on force "from the very beginning".

Maintaining Russian public opinion was firmly opposed to any alliance expansion, Rodionov hinted Moscow's position could change as growing cooperation with NATO changed the public perception of its former Cold War foe.
"We may support this idea when our public is convinced that NATO has indeed passed through a genuine transformation in accordance with the new conditions of the political situation."
Before meeting Rodionov, Perry told reporters enlargement would begin in 1997.
"At a summit next year several countries will be invited to start accession talks," he said.
Perry declined to be drawn on which countries may be invited to join the alliance, but emphasised the process would go ahead whatever Moscow's concerns.
"If I thought that those actions (expansion) were threatening Russia I would have a very different view, but I don't believe that for a minute," Perry said.

Since the end of the Cold War, ex-Communist countries have been seeking to join NATO to guarantee their future security against Russia. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the most likely candidates, but could be joined by Slovenia.

NATO is hoping also it can entice Russia to take part actively in the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme designed to try and fill a security vacuum in central and eastern Europe created by the collapse of communism.
The alliance wants to upgrade PFP and offer it as an alternative to countries left out of next year's expansion, but which still want an insurance policy against a rebirth of an expansionist Russia.

"What we are doing with NATO and what we are doing with Partnership for Peace is creating a security circle for all of Europe... our goal is not to threaten Russia, but to bring Russia into that security circle," Perry said.

NATO diplomats say the aim is to try to dovetail approval of both enlargement and a new pact for Russia at next year's heads of government summit which would also endorse reform of the alliance's command structures.
